issues.legal_issue: A will giving a widow enjoyment of property during her lifetime and giving the whole estate absolutely to a later beneficiary creates an ordinary life estate rather than a Hindu widow’s estate when the will and surrounding circumstances do not show that the widow received the broader powers of a Hindu widow.
material_facts: The will directed the widow to enjoy the entire estate only during her lifetime and then directed that the daughter and her heirs enjoy the same estate absolutely, with powers of alienation.
The will did not expressly give the widow power to alienate the estate, and the circumstances did not imply such a power for the stated obligations.
The estate produced sufficient income for the widow to meet the obligations mentioned in the will, and the evidence did not show that she needed to alienate the estate to do so.
The widow later sold and settled properties, and the plaintiff sought a declaration that those alienations would not bind the estate beyond her lifetime.
issues.conclusion: The widow received an ordinary life estate, not a Hindu widow’s estate; her alienations would not endure beyond her lifetime.
issues.legal_principle: The primary task in construing a Hindu will is to ascertain the testator’s intention from its language and the surrounding circumstances, including the testator’s family relationships and ordinary notions about the devolution of property. A Hindu may confer a limited life estate rather than the estate a widow would take by inheritance. A Hindu widow’s estate should not be inferred without language or necessary implication giving the widow the corresponding power to alienate for necessity; her powers under Hindu law are wider than powers limited to paying debts, maintenance, and other specified obligations. The court cautioned against construing differently worded wills by analogy, referring to Sasiman v. Shib Narain, and considered Mahomed Shumsool v. Shewukram and Mst. Bhagwati Devi v. Choudry Bholonath Thakur, among other authorities.

rule.if: hindu_will_dispute and widow_lifetime_only_language and gift_over_entire_estate_absolute and no_broad_alienation_power and income_sufficient_for_obligations

predicates.hindu_will_dispute: The dispute concerns the construction of a Hindu testator’s will governing the interests of a widow and a later beneficiary.
predicates.widow_lifetime_only_language: The will limits the widow’s enjoyment of the property to her lifetime.
predicates.gift_over_entire_estate_absolute: The will directs that the same entire estate pass after the widow’s lifetime to a later beneficiary with absolute ownership.
predicates.no_broad_alienation_power: The will does not expressly or by necessary implication give the widow the broad power to alienate the estate for purposes recognized under Hindu law.
predicates.income_sufficient_for_obligations: The estate’s income was sufficient to meet the obligations specified for the widow without alienating the estate.

issues.definition: When a Hindu will limits a widow’s enjoyment to her lifetime, gives the entire estate absolutely to a later beneficiary, and does not confer broad alienation powers despite sufficient income to meet specified obligations, the widow takes an ordinary life estate.

issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s future interest under a will vests when the will takes effect if the beneficiary is identified with certainty and the gift is not conditional on surviving the prior life tenant.
material_facts: The will identified the daughter and her heirs as the absolute beneficiaries of the entire estate after the widow’s lifetime.
The daughter was alive when the testator died but died before the widow, and none of her children survived her.
The plaintiff was the daughter’s husband and sole heir, and he claimed through her vested interest.
issues.conclusion: The daughter obtained a vested interest in the estate on the testator’s death, and that interest passed to her husband on her death.
issues.legal_principle: The law leans in favour of vesting, and a gift of future enjoyment vests when the will takes effect where the beneficiary and the property are identified with certainty and vesting is not made conditional on surviving the prior life tenant. The court relied on the principle stated in Jarman on Wills and distinguished a contingent expectancy under Hindu law from a present vested right to future enjoyment.

rule.if: hindu_will_dispute and later_beneficiary_certain and gift_covers_entire_estate and gift_not_conditional_on_survival

predicates.hindu_will_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an interest created by a Hindu testator’s will vested in a later beneficiary.
predicates.later_beneficiary_certain: The will identifies the later beneficiary with certainty.
predicates.gift_covers_entire_estate: The will gives the later beneficiary the entire estate after the prior life tenant’s interest ends.
predicates.gift_not_conditional_on_survival: The will does not make the later beneficiary’s gift conditional on surviving the prior life tenant.

issues.definition: When a Hindu will identifies a later beneficiary and gives that beneficiary the entire estate after a prior life interest without requiring survival of the prior life tenant, the future interest vests when the will takes effect and passes to the beneficiary’s heir.
